/*
# SimpleLayout — stack children along an axis

The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along
`axis`, in child order, `spacing` apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis
and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row
with the ordinary `y = center`. Invisible children are skipped and their
space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the slot it would occupy, so
re-showing it needs no special case. A `Spacer` child flexes to absorb the
run's slack along the axis (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on
each side centers the run).

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one
pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ]
    ]
```

## axis
Which way children stack: `y` (the default) or `x`. **A bare literal, not a string** —
`axis = x`, and note that `x` here is the axis token, not the position attribute.

## spacing
The gap between adjacent children. **Negative overlaps them**, which is how a stack of
cards or avatars is built.

## align
The **cross axis** — `y` on a row, `x` on a stack. `none` (the default) leaves it to the
children, who place themselves with the ordinary `y = center`. `start | center | end`
aligns every child within the **band**: the view's own cross extent — so a column
`width = 260` centres a `width = { parent.width - 32 }` child at 16, with the inset split
evenly — falling back to the **line**, the tallest (widest) laid child's extent, on a view
that derives its own cross size from these very children (reading an extent this
arrangement feeds would be a cycle, and on such a view the line *is* that extent). A
child wider than the band keeps the line, so it never hangs out both sides.
`baseline` — a row only — sits every child on one
baseline: a `Text` reports its own, and a composite **declares** which part carries it
(`baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }`); a laid child that declares none is
refused by name, at the child, and the checker says so before anything runs. A bare
literal.

## place()
The whole strategy: one box per laid child, positioned along the axis in child order.
**Every size stays the children's own, and so does the cross axis unless `align` says
otherwise** — then the boxes carry that slot too, and own it. Override it in a subclass
for custom geometry; a `Layout`'s `place()` **may** aggregate over children, which is the
one place that is allowed.
*/

class SimpleLayout extends Layout [
    axis: Axis = y,
    spacing: number = 0,
    align: CrossAlign = none,

    place() {
        const axis = this.axis
        const size = axis == "x" ? "width" : "height"
        const kids = this.laid()
        const flexing = (c) => (c).flexes === true

        // slack, only when someone flexes: the view's extent along the axis
        // minus the rigid content and the gaps between visible children.
        // A child's slot is its footprint (the scale/rotation-composed box),
        // so a scale = 0.5 child occupies half the run and a rotated card
        // reserves what it visibly covers; the box's lead compensates the
        // transform's own offset so the visible edge lands on the slot
        let each = 0
        let flexN = 0
        for (const c of kids) if (c.visible && flexing(c)) flexN = flexN + 1
        if (flexN > 0) {
            let content = 0
            let visN = 0
            for (const c of kids) {
                if (!c.visible) continue
                visN = visN + 1
                if (!flexing(c)) content = content + (c).footprint()[size]
            }
            const extent = this.view == null ? 0 : (this.view)[size]
            each = Math.max(0, (extent - content - this.spacing * Math.max(0, visN - 1)) / flexN)
        }

        // the cross axis, when `align` claims it: children align within the
        // BAND — the view's own cross extent, or the largest laid cross extent
        // when the view measures these very children (viewExtent answers 0 on
        // that view: reading an extent this pass feeds is the cycle the
        // one-pass discipline forbids, and there the two agree anyway).
        // Math.max keeps an over-wide child from hanging out both sides.
        // A baseline line is the deepest declared one.
        const al = this.align
        const cross = axis == "x" ? "y" : "x"
        const crossSize = axis == "x" ? "height" : "width"
        let line = 0
        let lineBase = 0
        if (al != "none") {
            if (al == "baseline" && axis != "x") this.refuseStackBaseline()
            for (const c of kids) {
                if (!c.visible) continue
                line = Math.max(line, (c).footprint()[crossSize])
                const b = (c).baseline
                if (al == "baseline" && typeof b == "number") lineBase = Math.max(lineBase, b)
            }
            // `start` places at the band's origin and `baseline` on the shared
            // line — neither reads the band, so only center/end ask for it
            if (al == "center" || al == "end") line = Math.max(line, this.viewExtent(crossSize))
        }

        let pos = 0
        return kids.map((c) => {
            const flex = c.visible && flexing(c)
            // footprint, never bounds: the strategy must not read the slot it
            // writes (one-pass discipline). A flexing child's size is allocated
            // (box.w/h), so its footprint is never consulted — lead 0, raw slot.
            const f = flex ? null : (c).footprint()
            const lead = f == null ? 0 : (axis == "x" ? f.x : f.y)
            const box = (axis == "x" ? ({ x: pos - lead }) : ({ y: pos - lead }))
            if (flex) box[axis == "x" ? "w" : "h"] = each
            if (al != "none") {
                // start = the line's origin; center/end offset the child's
                // footprint within the line; baseline sits the child's declared
                // baseline on the line's — a child with none is refused, once,
                // and placed at start (the arrangement never breaks)
                const fc = f == null ? (c).footprint() : f
                const leadC = axis == "x" ? fc.y : fc.x
                let off = 0
                if (al == "center") off = (line - fc[crossSize]) / 2
                else if (al == "end") off = line - fc[crossSize]
                else if (al == "baseline" && axis == "x") {
                    const b = (c).baseline
                    if (typeof b == "number") off = lineBase - b
                    else if (c.visible) this.refuseBaseline(c)
                }
                box[cross] = off - (al == "baseline" ? 0 : leadC)
            }
            if (c.visible) pos = pos + (flex ? each : (f)[size]) + this.spacing
            return box
            })
        }
    ]

/*
# ResponsiveLayout — arrange children differently at different widths.

A view's children often want one arrangement when there is room and another
when there isn't: three panels side by side on a wide screen, the same panels
stacked on a phone; an optional control that appears only when space allows.
ResponsiveLayout states those alternatives directly. You give it a list of
**plans** — each one says *"from this width up, arrange the children like
this"* — and it keeps the right plan applied as the view's width changes.
Hiding, showing, and dividing the width are all part of a plan, not separate
wiring.

    bar: View [
        layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [
            { from: 900, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 15, nav: 55, actions: 30 } },
            { from: 600, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 20, nav: 80, actions: 0 } },
            { from: 0,   flow: "stack" },
        ] } ],
        logo:    Logo    [ ],
        nav:     Nav     [ ],
        actions: Actions [ ],
    ]

Each entry's `from` means *use this plan when the view is at least this wide*
— the entry with the largest `from` that fits wins, wherever it sits in the
list, and an entry with `from: 0` is the fallback for anything narrower.
`flow` is the arrangement: `"row"` places children left to right; `"stack"`
places them top to bottom. `share` divides the width (what is left of it
after the gaps) among the children it names — the names are the view's own
child names, checked when the layout first arranges (a name with no child is
a loud error). `logo: 15` gives logo 15% of it; **`0` hides that child while
the plan is active** — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is just a
number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the view
widens. A child a plan does not name is left alone: natural width, the flow
just places it. `gap` sets the space between children (an entry may carry
its own `gap` to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children
keep their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as
always.

So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split
15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room;
below 600, everything stacks.

**Slack and alignment.** When a row's children keep natural widths, the run
may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a
knob: a `Spacer [ ]` child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes
them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it. On
the axis the flow does not manage, a child places itself with the ordinary
literals (`y = center` in a row). Shares that fill the width leave no slack
at all — *shares fill; naturals align.*

**Nesting — who decides what.** A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's
width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child
gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has
its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically.
Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct
children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.)

**Division of labor.** ResponsiveLayout manages **named regions**. A collection
of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool:
`WrappingLayout` (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width
constraint on the card.

**When the rules aren't enough.** A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap.
Whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a `State` applied on a
width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding `place()` —
the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

## plan
The storyboard: a list of `{ from, flow, share?, gap? }` entries. **`from` means "use
this plan when the view is at least this wide"** — the largest `from` that fits wins,
wherever it sits in the list, and `from: 0` is the fallback. `flow` is `"row"` or
`"stack"`. `share` divides the width among the children it **names by their own child
names**, checked when the layout first arranges — a name with no child is a loud error.
**A share of `0` hides that child while the plan is active**, so "the actions disappear
on small screens" is one number, and they return by themselves when the view widens. A
child a plan does not name keeps its natural width.

## gap
The default space between children, overridable per plan entry.

## place()
Selects the active plan from the **view's own width — never the window's** — and
arranges accordingly. That is what makes nesting work: the parent's plan decides how much
room a child gets, and the child's own plan answers to the room it got, automatically. A
plan can only name direct children; managing a grandchild is the child's plan's business.
*/

class ResponsiveLayout extends Layout [
    plan: array = { [] },
    gap: number = 10,

    place() {
        const view = this.view
        const W = view.width
        const kids = this.laid()
        const plans = (Array.isArray(this.plan) ? this.plan : [])

        // The active plan: the largest `from` that fits, wherever it sits in
        // the list; nothing fits → the smallest `from` (the nearest regime).
        let tier = null
        for (const t of plans) { const f = t.from ?? 0; if (W >= f && (tier == null || f > (tier.from ?? 0))) tier = t }
        if (tier == null) for (const t of plans) { if (tier == null || (t.from ?? 0) < (tier.from ?? 0)) tier = t }
        if (tier == null) tier = ({ flow: "row" })

        const stack = tier.flow == "stack"
        const gap = typeof tier.gap == "number" ? tier.gap : this.gap
        const share = tier.share != null && typeof tier.share == "object" ? tier.share : ({})

        // Resolve the share names against the view's own children — loudly.
        const shares = new Map()
        for (const name of Object.keys(share)) {
            const c = view[name]
            if (c == null || kids.indexOf(c) < 0) {
                throw new Error("the plan names '" + name + "', but " + view.constructor.name + " has no laid child named '" + name + "'")
            }
            shares.set(c, share[name])
        }

        const hidden = (c) => shares.get(c) === 0
        const flexing = (c) => (c).flexes === true && !hidden(c)

        // What the shares divide: the width left after the gaps between the
        // visible children (row flow); in a stack a share is simply a percent
        // of the view's width — heights are never touched by shares.
        let visN = 0
        for (const c of kids) if (c.visible && !hidden(c)) visN = visN + 1
        const avail = W - gap * Math.max(0, visN - 1)
        const shareW = (c) => (stack ? W : avail) * (shares.get(c)) / 100

        // Rigid content along the flow axis, to size the spacers: widths in a
        // row (a share is a width), the children's own heights in a stack.
        let rigid = 0
        let flexN = 0
        for (const c of kids) {
            if (!c.visible || hidden(c)) continue
            if (flexing(c)) { flexN = flexN + 1; continue }
            // natural sizes are the footprint (scale/rotation composed,
            // position-free); a share or flex allocation stays the raw slot it
            // claims — the strategy never reads a slot it writes
            rigid = rigid + (stack ? (c).footprint().height : (shares.has(c) ? shareW(c) : (c).footprint().width))
        }
        const room = stack ? view.height - gap * Math.max(0, visN - 1) : avail
        const each = flexN > 0 ? Math.max(0, room - rigid) / flexN : 0

        let pos = 0
        return kids.map((c) => {
            if (hidden(c)) {
                // excluded from the flow entirely: hidden, space reclaimed
                return stack ? ({ y: pos, vis: false }) : ({ x: pos, vis: false })
            }
            // allocated children (share, flex) take their slot raw; natural
            // ones are placed by footprint, lead-compensated
            const natural = !flexing(c) && !(stack ? false : shares.has(c))
            const f = natural ? (c).footprint() : null
            const lead = f == null ? 0 : (stack ? f.y : f.x)
            const box = (stack ? ({ y: pos - lead }) : ({ x: pos - lead }))
            if (shares.has(c)) box.w = shareW(c)                       // a share allocates width, both flows
            if (flexing(c)) box[stack ? "h" : "w"] = each              // a spacer flexes along the flow axis
            const adv = flexing(c) ? each
                      : stack      ? (f).height
                      : shares.has(c) ? shareW(c) : (f).width
            if (c.visible) pos = pos + adv + gap
            return box
            })
        }
    ]

/*
# Spacer — a flexing child that absorbs a run's slack

When a row (or stack) does not fill its container, the leftover space has to
go somewhere — and the laid children cannot take it themselves (their
flow-axis slot is owned by the layout). A Spacer says where, structurally: put one between two
groups and they push apart ("logo left, actions right"); put one on each
side of a run and it centers; put one first and the run right-aligns.
Several spacers split the slack evenly. When there is no slack — a plan
whose shares fill the width, an auto-sized container — a Spacer is simply
zero and invisible in effect.

The layout owns a Spacer's flow-axis size (a percent-family constraint, so
a container deriving its extent from its children never counts one); the
`flexes` marker is what a flow layout looks for. An empty view otherwise —
it paints nothing and has no size of its own.

## flexes
The marker a flow layout looks for. True (the default) means the layout owns this
Spacer's size along the flow axis and expands it to take up the slack — which is
what makes `Spacer [ ]` push its siblings apart. Set it false for a fixed gap you
size yourself.
*/

class Spacer extends View [
    flexes: boolean = true,
    width = 0,
    height = 0
    ]

/*
# Control

The interaction-state base every stateful control extends. It owns how the pointer, keyboard, and focus relate to this view — and
nothing semantic: `checked`, `value`, and their kin live on the concrete control.

The pointer half is the language's: `hovered` and `pressed` are View's read-only
interaction intrinsics (chain-based, touch-correct, cancel-safe). What Control adds is
the control policy on top of them, as derivations every concrete control reads:

- `hot` / `down` — the styling pair: the intrinsics gated by `disabled`, with the
  keyboard-activation `flash` folded into `down`. Style against these, not the raw
  intrinsics, and a disabled control never lights up.
- `disabled` — inert: not focusable, no activation; concrete controls gate on it.
- keyboard — Space or Enter on the focused control activates it, the same `press()`
  path a pointer uses, acknowledged by flashing the pressed look.

It also owns two things every labelled control shares:

- `iconLeft` / `iconRight` — decoration, by class name. A concrete control lays
  them out; Control only declares that they exist, so every control that shows
  one names it the same way.
- `menu` — the **role** of dropping a menu, not decoration. Setting `menu` gets
  the disclosure mark, the anchored open, the held-open styling, and
  ArrowDown-to-open together, which is the part a hand-rolled copy gets wrong
  one piece at a time.

Extend it to make your own control a first-class one — focusable, keyboard-activated,
and styled off the same state pair as everything the library ships:

```declare
class Stepper extends Control [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6,
    n: number = 0,
    fill = { down ? theme.controlPressed : hot ? theme.controlHover : theme.control },
    press() { n = n + 1 },
    onClick() { if (!disabled) press() },
    t: TextLabel [ x = center, fontSize = 13, text = { "" + classroot.n } ]
    ]


App [ Stepper [ x = 20, y = 20 ] ]
```

## theme
The design-token record every widget styles off — a **provided value**. An app
provides it once (`App [ theme = { app.dark ? SanFranciscoDark : SanFrancisco } ]`)
and `Control` reads it here, so a control body reads `theme.accent` as a plain,
typed member. The default is `SanFrancisco`, so a control in an app that never
mentions a theme still renders. Provide a different record on a subtree to reskin
it; every `provided("theme")` below reads the nearer one.

## disabled
Inert: not focusable, no activation, and the gate folded into `hot`/`down` so a
disabled control never lights up. **Constrain it rather than assigning it**
(`disabled = { app.muted }`) — it is ordinary derived state. Concrete controls also
dim themselves against `theme.disabledOpacity`.

## hot
Hover under control policy — `hovered` gated by `disabled`. **Style against this, not
the raw `hovered` intrinsic**, or a disabled control lights up under the pointer. Always
false on touch, since `hovered` is.

## down
The pressed look — the `pressed` intrinsic gated by `disabled`, **with keyboard
activation folded in**, so Space/Enter flashes the same appearance a pointer press
gives. The other half of the styling pair with `hot`.

## focused
True while this control holds keyboard focus. For the *ring*, you want nothing: the
app-level `FocusRing` indicates focus for you. Read this only for a control's own
focus styling.

## focusVisible
Focused **and** the focus arrived by keyboard — the web's `:focus-visible` channel.
Cleared by blur and by a pointer press on this control, so a clicked control shows no
keyboard edge while a tabbed one does. What a `Pane` header's focus edge reads.

## iconLeft
A decorative icon for the leading slot, **named by class** (`iconLeft = "TrashIcon"`),
not nested as a child — a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form where authored
and data-bound are the same mechanism (`iconLeft = { "" + :icon }` in a replicated
toolbar). Control only declares the slot; the concrete control lays it out. A
**computed** name needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build, since no static reference
reaches it.

## iconRight
The trailing icon slot, same vocabulary as `iconLeft`. Setting it **wins over the
chevron a `menu` would imply** — see `rightIcon`.

## menu
The menu this control drops — an instance, not a name (`menu = { app.optionsMenu }`).
Setting it is a *role*, not decoration: the disclosure mark, the anchored open below
the control, the held-open fill, and ArrowDown-to-open all follow together. **Declare
one menu and point many controls at it** rather than one per opener; the menu reads
`opener` to vary its items.

## menuOpen
True while `menu` is showing *and* this control is what opened it. **Derived, never
written** — a flag set on open goes stale the moment the menu closes some other way
(Escape, a pick, a press on the backdrop) and strands the control in its held-open
look forever.

## rightIcon
What actually renders on the right: `iconRight` when set, else the disclosure chevron
implied by `menu`, else nothing. One place decides, so every menu-dropping control
wears the same mark.

## flash
The keyboard-activation pulse — the control's own state, since the `pressed` intrinsic
is the pointer's truth and is read-only. Folded into `down`, so styling needs to read
only the pair.

## flashMs
How long `flashPress()` holds the pressed look.

## openMenu()
Opens `menu` anchored to this control, unless there is none or the control is disabled.
The seam a concrete control calls from its own `press()`.

## press()
**The activation seam — override this, not the handlers.** Pointer and keyboard both
land here, so one override serves a click, Space, and Enter. The base opens `menu` when
there is one. A value control delivers through `input` from here and **never writes its
own value slot directly**, which is what lets a bound control avoid fighting its
constraint.

## focusShape()
The focus silhouette the ring hugs, `{ x, y, w, h, rad }` in this control's own
coordinates. `null` (the default) rings the whole bounds at its `cornerRadius`. Override
to ring the part that means something — a `Radio` rings its dot, a `Slider` its thumb.

## flashPress()
Flashes the pressed look to acknowledge keyboard activation — the platform convention
for buttons and menu items. **Value controls whose state change is itself the feedback
(Checkbox, Switch, Radio) deliberately do not call it.**

## onFocus
Records focus and captures the keyboard modality into `focusVisible`. An override must
keep both or the focus channel goes dark.

## onBlur
Clears `focused` and `focusVisible`.

## onPointerDown
Claims focus, clears the `:focus-visible` channel, and opens `menu` if there is one —
menus open on **press**, not release, as the platform does. **An override must keep the
`Focus.focus(this)` call**, or clicking the control strands the keyboard elsewhere.

## onKeyDown
Space and Enter run `press()`; ArrowDown opens `menu`. Ignores auto-repeat.

## focusable
A control takes focus unless it is disabled — one rule, so a disabled control drops out of the Tab order without saying so twice.
*/

class Control extends View [
    // The design-token record every widget styles off — a provided value: the
    // app provides it once (`App [ theme = { … } ]`) and Control reads it here,
    // so a widget body reads `theme.accent` as a plain, typed member. The
    // default is `SanFrancisco`, so a widget in an app that never mentions a
    // theme still renders — the visible library default.

    theme: Theme = { this.$provided("theme", SanFrancisco) },

    disabled: boolean = false,
    focused:  boolean = false,

    // A control is chrome, not prose: its label never selects, even inside a
    // `selectable` region (a provision here vetoes the inherited value — the
    // language rule: anything that activates declares itself unselectable).

    selectable = false,

    // the styling pair — the interaction intrinsics under control policy

    hot:  boolean = { this.hovered && !this.disabled },
    down: boolean = { (this.pressed && !this.disabled) || this.flash },

    // The :focus-visible channel for the control's own styling (a Tab header's
    // focus edge): focused and the focus arrived by keyboard. Captured at the
    // focus event (the web's rule), cleared by blur — and by a pointer press on
    // this very control, the one case with no focus event (Focus.focus on the
    // already-focused target is a no-op, but the modality still cleared).

    focusVisible: boolean = false,

    focusable = { !this.disabled },

    // The keyboard affordance is the app-level FocusRing (focusring.declare —
    // one traveling indicator, declared once in the App), not a per-control
    // ring; `focused` stays declared here for controls' own styling.

    // ── content slots ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    //
    // Icons by class name, resolved through the tag registry. A name rather than
    // a child because a control is a leaf — everything else about it is an
    // attribute — and because an attribute is the one form where authored and
    // bound are the same mechanism: `iconLeft = TrashIcon` and
    // `iconLeft = { "" + :icon }` in a replicated toolbar are one slot.

    iconLeft:  string = "",
    iconRight: string = "",

    // The menu this control drops. Set it and the disclosure mark, the anchored
    // open, and the open-state styling all follow; `openMenu()` is the seam a
    // concrete control calls from its own `press()`.

    menu: View = null,

    // Derived, not written. A flag set on open goes stale the moment the menu
    // closes some other way — Escape, a pick, a click on the backdrop — and the
    // button keeps its held-open fill for the rest of the session. Reading the
    // menu's own state cannot drift: it is open if the menu is shown and this
    // control is what opened it (one menu serves many openers).

    menuOpen: boolean = { this.menu != null
                       && (this.menu).shown === true
                       && (this.menu).opener === this },

    // What a control shows on the right: an explicit icon wins, else the
    // disclosure chevron a `menu` implies. One place decides, so every
    // menu-dropping control wears the same mark.

    rightIcon: string = { this.iconRight != "" ? this.iconRight : this.menu != null ? "ChevronIcon" : "" },

    openMenu() {
        if (this.menu == null || this.disabled) return
        ;(this.menu).openFor(this)
        },

    // the activation seam — concrete controls override; pointer and keyboard both land here

    press() { if (this.menu != null) this.openMenu() },

    // the control's focus silhouette — override to ring something other than
    // the whole bounds (a Radio rings its dot). null = bounds + cornerRadius.
    // { x, y, w, h, rad } in the control's own coordinates.

    focusShape() { return null },

    // keyboard activation's visual acknowledgment: flash the pressed look, the
    // platform convention for buttons. Value controls whose state change is
    // the feedback (Checkbox, Switch, Radio) don't call this. `flashMs` is
    // per-control tunable. `flash` is the control's own state — the `pressed`
    // intrinsic is the pointer's truth and is read-only; a keyboard pulse is a
    // different fact, folded into `down`.

    flash:   boolean = false,
    flashMs: number  = 220,

    flashPress() {
        this.flash = true
        setTimeout(() => { this.flash = false }, this.flashMs)
        },

    onFocus() { this.focused = true; this.focusVisible = Focus.byKeyboard() },
    onBlur()  { this.focused = false; this.focusVisible = false },

    // A click is also a focus claim — the keyboard picks up where the pointer
    // left. A menu opens here, not from `onClick`: every other control routes
    // the pointer through `press()` (`onClick() { if (!disabled) press() }`),

# Icon — the drawn mark

A small monochrome mark, **drawn** rather than typed. A font's glyphs are not
marks: they are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on
every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a `✓` sits on the
text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The
library's own marks — `Checkbox.mark`, `Menu.check`, the `Combobox` disclosure —
are all `Icon`s.

### Writing one

Subclass and override `draw`. Author the shape in a **16×16 box** — `unit`
converts it to whatever size the host asked for:

```declare-fragment
class SparkIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(unit, unit)
        d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit
        d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke()
        }
    ]
```

Overriding a **method** is the refinement path that works — re-opening an
inherited child is not (`cap:` on a `Button` subclass fails at instantiate), so
the shape lives in `draw` and everything adjustable is a slot.

### Size changes the drawing, not the shape

Every icon is **one path**. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing
redrawn at a breakpoint: `unit` scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for,
so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly.

The **stroke** is the deliberate exception. `d.lineWidth = weight / unit` sits
*inside* `d.scale(unit, unit)`, so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant
`weight` in **device pixels at every size**. An icon's line therefore matches the
1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows.

The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5%
at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px — chrome sizes — that is invisible. Past ~32
an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a mark — so **this set
is built for chrome sizes**, and a large display icon (an empty-state mark, an
about-box graphic) would want the opposite: `d.lineWidth = weight` *outside* the
scale, so the line grows with the drawing. Real icon systems take a third road
and redraw per optical size range; that is a bigger undertaking than this set
needs.

### What is not an Icon

Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before
reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification
swell, they are polychrome (`gradient(hue1, hue2)` behind a hue-parameterised
drawing), and their **width animates every frame**. Each of those alone rules
them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and
reads spindly; `ink` is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing
this set forbids.

The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is
**chrome vocabulary versus identity**. A mark that says *close*, *expand*,
*checked*, *this is the dark theme* belongs here, at a size the host states.
A mark that says *this is Calendar* does not, and belongs to the app that owns
the identity.

Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows
take `WindowIcon` and `CodeIcon` from this set, while its dock keeps `DockIcon`.

### Two rules

**Scale inside the body, never with the View's `scale`.** A recording rasterizes
into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution, while `scale` is
a transform applied *after* — so `scale = { width / 16 }` would rasterize 16
pixels and stretch them. Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is
most of them. Scaling inside the recording allocates the raster at true size
instead.

**Never animate an icon's `width`.** Reading size inside `draw` makes the
recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records **and** reallocates the
backing canvas every frame, which drops a magnifying dock of icons from 60 to
~25fps. A static size re-records once and costs nothing after: 120 icons
re-recording their *content* every frame run frame-bound at 16.6ms, cheaper
than the 120 text glyphs they replace.

Colour is not a rule — `ink` follows the provided text colour, so an icon beside
a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a
menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

## ink
The mark's colour. Follows the provided `textColor`, so an icon beside a muted

## isIcon
**Internal.** The marker a layout keys on to place an icon without knowing which shape

## height
Square, always — the height follows the width.

## iconSize

## textColor
The effective text colour the mark's `ink` follows — a **provided value**, so an icon

A horizontal flow that **wraps**: children run left to right `spacing` apart,
and when the next one would overflow the view's width it drops to a new row

one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it stacks — cards that reflow
on a phone with no media query. It owns both axes of each child (a flow is
2-D); sizes stay the children's own. `justify`
sets each finished row along the flow — `start`, `center`, `end`, or `fill`,
which spreads a row's slack into its gaps the way justified text does;
`indent` and `hangingIndent` inset the first row and every row after it, the
two shapes a paragraph takes.

that reflow by fitting. Managing named regions per width tier is
ResponsiveLayout's.

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place().

```declare
box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, lineSpacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ]
```

The horizontal gap between children in a row.

## lineSpacing
The vertical gap between rows. **`-1` (the default) means "same as `spacing`"**, so a
uniform grid needs one number rather than two kept in step.

## justify
How a finished row sits along the flow: `start` (the default, left), `center`, `end`
(right), or `fill` — the row's slack is spread evenly into the gaps between its
children, so every full row ends flush at the right edge, as justified text does. As
in text, the last row is left at `start` under `fill` (a ragged last line), and a row
of one child has no gap to widen and stays put. A bare literal.

## indent
The first row's inset from the left, in pixels — a paragraph's first-line indent. The
first row's usable width shrinks by it; later rows are unaffected (see `hangingIndent`).

## hangingIndent
The inset of every row after the first — a hanging indent, the shape of a bibliography
entry or a wrapped signature whose continuation lines step in under the name. The two
compose: `indent` sets where the first row starts, `hangingIndent` where the rest do.

# AppIsland — a whole Declare program running inside a box

`AppIsland` embeds a live Declare application: give it a `program` and it mounts
that program as its own child app — its own reactive graph, input router, and
stage — sized to this view's box. There is no coordinate sync: the tenant fills
the box, so your width/height constraints size it like any view.

It composes `DOMIsland` (the sanctioned foreign-content leaf) and builds the
host's mount key from structured inputs, so callers never hand-splice the
`run:…` wire. The page host (`browser/host-client.js`) sees the key on the box,
resolves the program on its boot ladder — prewarm → cache → in-browser compile,
identical on the dev server and a static host — and renders the child.

`childName` (inherited from `DOMIsland`) is the reverse channel: the running child's
`appName` reflected back up, so a host can title itself by what it shows.

### The bridge

An AppIsland carries the **island bridge** (guide ch. 18): declare `external`
attributes on the instance and they pair, by name and with a type handshake,
against the tenant program's own `external` declarations — typed facts both
ways, per settle. `post(topic, payload)` / `onPost(m: IslandPost)` carry the
verbs. `env` and `childName` below are untyped channels beside the bridge;
declare `external` attributes wherever the type matters.

The window frame, activation, and titling belong to the caller — a desktop window
adds an `onPointerDown` that raises itself and reads `childName` for its title; the
homepage and the viewer just size the box. This primitive is only the embedding.

## program
What to run: a program name, a relative path (`"../../calendar/calendar"` reaches the
real app — **no copy of the source, ever**), or the reserved `"__raw__"` live-edit
channel, where the running program is the host app's `liveSource` and recompiles as it
changes. **`""` detaches the island** and nothing mounts, which is how a closed panel
stops paying for its tenant — and what bounds the recursion when a program embeds a
view of itself.

## env
The embedding environment in query form (`"dark=1&base=../x/"`), delivered to the
child's reactive `app.env` at mount **and on every change**. Empty sends none, so the
child keeps its own defaults — leave it alone unless the host genuinely overrides
something, or you will pin the child's appearance against the system's.

## slot
The host's slot marker, derived from `program` and `env` — `run:<program>|<env>` — which is what the island host wires. Nothing to set by hand.
*/

class AppIsland extends DOMIsland [
    program: string = "",
    env: string = "",

    // program → empty slot → the island stays detached (DOMIsland unmounts it).

    slot = { this.program == "" ? "" : "run:" + this.program + (this.env == "" ? "" : "|" + this.env) }

the focused control and reshapes to its own silhouette on arrival. The ring springs
position, size **and** `cornerRadius` together, which is why a Radio's row ring, a

  so the next Tab's flight departs from the control the user just clicked,
  never from a stale perch.

  theme-and-components pair). While keyboard modality holds and the role
  includes rest, the ring rests — no idle fade; a pointer press clears
  modality and the ring hides (web :focus-visible semantics).

never a pointer target. The silhouette is the target's `focusShape()` when it
declares one, else its bounds at its `cornerRadius`.

below and watch it fly; the members exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition,
and for the theme tokens that elect its behaviour.

```declare
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 12 ],
    Button [ label = "One" ],
    Button [ label = "Two" ],
    Checkbox [ label = "Three" ]
```

Whether the ring is visible. **A pointer focus parks it silently** — geometry current,
ring hidden — so the next Tab departs from the control the user just clicked rather
than from a stale perch.

because a flight from nowhere is a streak across the app.

not to the ring alone.

Whether the elected role includes resting — a resting ring does not idle-fade.

Whether the elected role includes the flight.

first appearance, and `theme.focusAnimate = false` all use — **and what a target moving

never sets it.

## ty

## tw

## th

## trad

/*
The blueprint backdrop is viewport-sized and follows the scroll, never
document-sized.

`draw()` rasterizes into a canvas the size of the view's bounds at device pixel
ratio, so a backdrop stretched over a whole document would allocate a backing
store for the whole document — tens of megapixels for the language view at 2x,
reallocated every time the view is shown or hidden, and past a browser's
maximum canvas dimension. One viewport costs one screen.

A uniform 32px lattice looks the same pinned as it does scrolling, so this
costs nothing visually — it is the same paper, drawn once. The view follows
the scroll rather than spanning the document: `ignoreScroll` would lift it out
of paint order and composite it over the content, while as an ordinary child
it stays behind. Its y snaps to the 32px lattice so the lines land where a
document-tall paper's would, and it is clamped to the content's own bottom
(`bottom`, the use site's extent): unclamped, the backdrop's bottom would be
scrollY plus a viewport, which feeds the scroller's auto-extent — every trip
to the bottom would grow the page another 32px. Reading the content's extent
is not a cycle: the content never reads the backdrop.
*/

class GridBg extends View [
    bottom: number = 0,
    x = 0, width = { this.root.width },
    y = { Math.max(0, Math.min(Math.floor(this.root.scrollY / 32) * 32, this.bottom - this.height)) },
    height = { this.root.height + 32 },
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.fillStyle = this.$provided("theme").grid
        for (let gx = 0; gx <= this.width;  gx += 32) d.fillRect(gx, 0, 1, this.height)
        for (let gy = 0; gy <= this.height; gy += 32) d.fillRect(0, gy, this.width, 1)
        }
    ]

    /* ## Fixed chrome

       `ignoreScroll` — the scroll carries everyone but these; they ride the
       window while the page's own scroll carries the content: the top bar, the
       pointer dot, the mobile nav sheet, and the Apps dropdown. */

    // the bar is always present, stuck to the top: a first-time visitor sees
    // the whole map

    header: View [ ignoreScroll = true, width = { this.root.width }, height = { 56 + this.root.safeTop }, y = 0, fill = { this.$provided("theme").surface },
        hairline: View [ y = { 55 + this.root.safeTop }, width = { this.root.width }, height = 1, fill = { this.$provided("theme").line } ],

        /* The header row, gutter to gutter. One ResponsiveLayout decides whether
           the pill row fits, and `share: 0` is the hiding — so there is no width
           test written by hand and no `visible` to keep in step with a number.
           Above the threshold the plan drops the kebab; below it the plan drops
           the pills and the kebab takes over, the whole list moving to the sheet.
           Nothing is ever dropped from the list itself, unlike a progressively
           trimmed pill row.

           The threshold is the row's own width, not the window's (a plan watches
           its view), and it is measured: the wordmark runs 53 and the pills 477,
           so 593 leaves 63 between them. It is also the one number that moves
           when `navItems` gains an entry — which is why it is stated once.

           The Spacer is what right-aligns the run: it absorbs the slack between
           the wordmark and whatever follows. Shares fill; naturals align. */

        bar: View [ x = { this.root.gutter }, y = { this.root.safeTop }, height = 56,
            width = { this.root.width - this.root.gutter * 2 },
            layout: ResponsiveLayout [ gap = 0, plan = { [
                ({ from: 593, flow: "row", share: ({ kebab: 0 }) }),
                ({ from: 0,   flow: "row", share: ({ nav: 0 }) })] } ],

            // wordmark — the product name in the brand gradient, in the hero's typeface

            brand: View [ y = 18, height = 22,
                layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 0 ],
                link = "#home",
                Heading [ fontSize = 15, textFill = { this.$provided("theme").brand }, text = "Declare" ]
                ],

            Spacer [ ],

            // primary nav — one NavLink per navItems entry; the padded pills carry
            // their own spacing

            nav: View [ y = 11,
                layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 2 ],
                datapath = { this.root.navSource.value },
                NavLink [ datapath = :items[], label = { this.$data(["label"]) }, menu = { this.$data(["children","length"]) > 0 },
                    link = { this.$data(["children","length"]) > 0 ? "" : this.$data(["link"]) } ]
                ],

            // the kebab — three stacked dots (the page's dot motif), the pill's own
            // press feedback, toggling the sheet

            kebab: View [ y = 11, width = 34, height = 33, cornerRadius = 8,
                fill = { this.pressed ? this.$provided("theme").pillPress : this.hovered ? this.$provided("theme").pillHover : null },
                onClick()     { this.root.menuOpen = !this.root.menuOpen },
                d1: View [ x = center, y = 8,  width = 3, height = 3, cornerRadius = 1.5, fill = { parent.hovered || parent.pressed ? this.$provided("theme").text : this.$provided("theme").muted } ],
                d2: View [ x = center, y = 15, width = 3, height = 3, cornerRadius = 1.5, fill = { parent.hovered || parent.pressed ? this.$provided("theme").text : this.$provided("theme").muted } ],
                d3: View [ x = center, y = 22, width = 3, height = 3, cornerRadius = 1.5, fill = { parent.hovered || parent.pressed ? this.$provided("theme").text : this.$provided("theme").muted } ]
                ]
            ]
        ],

    // pointer dot — a 10px teal dot in viewport space that springs after the
    // pointer (loose + low-mass = the slower, longer trail). Two position
    // Springs; the native cursor stays visible and leads, the dot follows.

    pointerDot: View [ ignoreScroll = true, width = 10, height = 10, cornerRadius = 5, fill = { this.$provided("theme").accentSecondary }, opacity = 0.9,
        shadow = { shadow(0, 0, 12, this.$provided("theme").accentSecondary) },

        // Decoration, not a target: the dot settles exactly under a resting
        // cursor, and the hit chain is occlusion-correct — without this line
        // the dot would swallow every hover and press the moment the mouse
        // stops.

        pointerEvents = "none",

        // Only for a hovering pointer (mouse / trackpad) — `app.hovering` is false
        // for touch, so the dot never appears on a phone, yet an iPad trackpad
        // (which reports a "mouse" pointer) still gets it. Also yields to the
        // native I-beam when the pointer is over an editable field.

        visible = { this.root.hovering && !this.root.pointerOverText },
        followX: Spring [ attribute = x, to = { this.root.pointerX - 5 },
            stiffness = 120, damping = 14, mass = 0.6, epsilon = 0.05 ],
        followY: Spring [ attribute = y, to = { this.root.pointerY - 5 },
            stiffness = 120, damping = 14, mass = 0.6, epsilon = 0.05 ]
        ],

    // the mobile nav sheet — the kebab's menu, above everything. A dim scrim below
    // the header catches an outside tap (and leaves the header + kebab lit, so the
    // kebab still toggles it shut); the top-right panel lists every destination as
    // a thumb-height row, replicated from the same navSource as the pills. Auto-hides
    // if the window is widened back past the breakpoint.

    navSheet: View [ ignoreScroll = true, visible = { this.root.menuOpen && this.root.header.bar.kebab.visible }, width = { this.root.width }, height = { this.root.height },
        scrim: View [ y = { 56 + this.root.safeTop }, width = { parent.width }, height = { parent.height - 56 - this.root.safeTop }, fill = { this.$provided("theme").scrim },
            onClick() { this.root.menuOpen = false }
            ],
        panel: View [ x = { this.root.width - this.root.gutter - this.width }, y = { 62 + this.root.safeTop }, width = 236, cornerRadius = 12,
            fill = { this.$provided("theme").surface }, shadow = { shadow(0, 12, 40, this.$provided("theme").shade) },

            // derived from the list, not counted: rows and group children are
            // not one uniform height, so a row count times a height would state
            // a relationship the sheet does not have

            height = { this.list.contentHeight + 12 },
            list: View [ x = 6, y = 6, width = { parent.width - 12 }, height = { this.contentHeight },
                layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 0 ],
                datapath = { this.root.navSource.value },
                MobileNavGroup [ datapath = :items[] ]
                ]
            ]
        ],

    // the Apps dropdown — the pill row's own menu, the same rows as the sheet
    // (MobileNavRow), anchored under the Apps pill. A transparent catcher
    // below closes it on an outside tap; narrowing past the breakpoint hides
    // it with the pills it belongs to.

    appsMenu: View [ ignoreScroll = true, visible = { this.root.appsOpen && !this.root.header.bar.kebab.visible },
        width = { this.root.width }, height = { this.root.height },
        catcher: View [ width = { parent.width }, height = { parent.height },
            onClick() { this.root.appsOpen = false }
            ],
        panel: View [ x = { this.root.appsX }, y = { this.root.appsY }, width = 190, cornerRadius = 12,
            fill = { this.$provided("theme").surface }, shadow = { shadow(0, 12, 40, this.$provided("theme").shade) },
            height = { this.list.contentHeight + 12 },
            list: View [ x = 6, y = 6, width = { parent.width - 12 }, height = { this.contentHeight },
                layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 0 ],
                datapath = { this.root.appsSource.value },
                MobileNavRow [ datapath = :items[], label = { this.$data(["label"]) }, link = { this.$data(["link"]) } ]
                ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
